common_name: Album White Bloody Cranesbill (Pure White Geranium sanguineum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Album keeps the same low mounding habit as the species but carries clean white flowers instead of magenta.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, where Album forms a tidy, finely cut mound and blooms heavily for weeks in early summer with a lighter repeat flush later if sheared. The pure white flowers give it a cooler, brighter effect than the species and make it a useful color break in mixed plantings of the more common magenta-pink bloody cranesbill. Like the species it tolerates poor, rocky, or dry soil once established and needs no staking. Shear the whole clump back by half after the main bloom to refresh the foliage and encourage a second round of flowers.

common_name: Spessart Bigroot Geranium (Pale Pink German-Bred Macrorrhizum Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil anywhere from full sun to full shade; Spessart is a vigorous, free-flowering bigroot selection named for the German forest region where it was raised.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in anything from full sun to fairly deep shade; Spessart bears an unusually heavy crop of soft pale pink flowers with prominent red calyces in late spring above aromatic, sticky, semi-evergreen foliage. It spreads by thick surface rhizomes into a dense, weed-smothering mat that handles dry shade and root competition from trees as well as any bigroot geranium, and is noted among gardeners for flowering more freely than some older bigroot cultivars. Fall color runs to orange and red on the retained foliage in mild winters. Established plantings need minimal water and only occasional division to keep the mat within bounds.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; grayleaf cranesbill is a small alpine species best sited in a rock garden, raised bed, or wall crevice where winter wet drains away quickly.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained, average to lean soil in full sun; grayleaf cranesbill forms a low cushion of rounded, deeply cut, gray-green leaves and carries shallow saucer-shaped flowers in shades of pink to purple with darker veining from late spring into summer. Its diminutive scale and preference for lean, fast-draining soil make it a natural for troughs, rock gardens, and wall crevices rather than mixed borders, where richer soil and competition cause it to rot or fade. It is the parent of several popular alpine hybrid geraniums and, like them, resents winter wet more than cold itself. Avoid mulching against the crown and skip supplemental water except during extended summer drought.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Dalmatian cranesbill hugs the ground on woody stems and is well suited to rock gardens, wall tops, or edging where its trailing habit can be appreciated.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Dalmatian cranesbill spreads on short woody stems into a low, glossy mat of rounded, lobed leaves that turn rich red and orange in fall, studded with clear pink flowers in late spring to early summer. It is more diminutive and slower-spreading than its relative bigroot geranium, making it a good choice for smaller spaces such as rock gardens, wall crevices, and path edges. Native to rocky Balkan hillsides, it tolerates drought and lean soil well once established and needs little care beyond an occasional tidy-up. It is one of the two parent species behind the popular Geranium x cantabrigiense groundcover hybrids.

common_name: Cambridge Geranium (Dalmaticum x Macrorrhizum Hybrid Groundcover Cranesbill)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; this naturally occurring garden hybrid between Geranium dalmaticum and Geranium macrorrhizum spreads steadily into a dense flowering mat.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; the Cambridge geranium combines the compact scale of Dalmatian cranesbill with the vigor and aromatic foliage of bigroot geranium, forming a dense, semi-evergreen carpet studded with pink to magenta flowers in late spring. It spreads by rhizome into a reliable, low-maintenance groundcover that tolerates dry shade, root competition from trees, and poor soil better than most flowering perennials, and its scented leaves largely deter deer and rabbits. Named cultivars selected from this cross, such as those with paler or deeper flower color, are grown far more often than the unnamed hybrid, but straight seedling or nursery stock is still occasionally offered under this name. An occasional shearing after bloom keeps the mat neat, and division every several years controls spread.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Karmina is the deepest-flowered of the widely grown Cambridge geranium cultivars and spreads at the same steady, groundcover-forming pace as Biokovo.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; Karmina bears a heavy late-spring flush of deep magenta-pink flowers, noticeably more saturated in color than the pale-pink or white-blushed cultivars more commonly sold, above the same aromatic, semi-evergreen, lobed foliage typical of the Cambridge geranium group. It forms a dense, weed-suppressing carpet that tolerates dry shade, root competition, and poor soil about as well as any hardy geranium, and its scented leaves are rarely browsed by deer or rabbits. Fall brings attractive orange-red foliage tones that often persist into winter in milder climates. Shear lightly after bloom to tidy the mat and divide overgrown patches every few years to renew vigor or start new plantings.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade to full sun; French cranesbill spreads steadily by rhizome and is the wild parent behind most of the popular Geranium x oxonianum garden hybrids.

directions: Plant in average, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade to full sun; French cranesbill produces a long season of clear pink, notched flowers from late spring well into summer above mounded, semi-evergreen foliage, and spreads readily by rhizome to fill space in a mixed border or light woodland edge. It is more shade-tolerant and moisture-loving than bloody cranesbill, and its willingness to hybridize freely with related species has produced most of the widely grown pink Oxonianum cultivars sold today. Left to its own devices it can spread more aggressively than gardeners expect in rich, damp soil, so give it room or plan to divide it periodically. Shearing spent flowering stems partway through summer often triggers a fresh flush of bloom into fall.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; pencilled cranesbill is a woodland-edge species that self-sows gently once established.

directions: Plant in average, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; pencilled cranesbill carries pale whitish to soft pink flowers finely traced with purple veins over glossy, lobed foliage from late spring into summer, giving it a delicate look distinct from the bolder pinks and magentas of most hardy geraniums. Native to woodland margins in southern Europe, it tolerates deeper shade than bloody or bigroot geranium and combines well with ferns and other shade perennials in a naturalistic planting. It self-sows modestly in favorable conditions without becoming a nuisance, and is one of the lesser-known parents contributing to some Oxonianum-type hybrid cultivars. Little care is needed beyond cutting back tired foliage in mid-summer to encourage fresh growth.
